name: Delivery Guarantees
intent: Know what a messaging system can actually promise (at-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once), what "exactly once" really means, and where the guarantee stops.
scenario: A consumer processes payment events from a log. For each event it charges a card and writes a ledger row. We crash it at different moments (before processing, after the card call, after the commit, with the ack lost) and watch which payments are lost, which are processed twice, and what the final state looks like against the intended one.
problem: Between a broker and a consumer there is a network and a process that can crash, and neither side can tell "the message was processed but the ack was lost" apart from "the message was never processed". So a broker must choose: forget the message after one try (it may be lost) or keep retrying until it hears an ack (it may be delivered twice). A pure exactly-once delivery is not available. What you can build is exactly-once effect, and only for effects that sit inside a system you control.

howItWorks.title: At-most-once: acknowledge first, process second
howItWorks.text: The broker marks the message done as soon as it is handed over (auto-ack, MQTT QoS 0, a Kafka offset committed before the work). If the consumer crashes before it finishes, the message is gone and nobody retries it. Nothing is ever duplicated, and nothing is guaranteed. That is fine for metrics samples and heartbeats, wrong for payments.

howItWorks.title: At-least-once: process first, acknowledge after
howItWorks.text: The broker keeps the message until the consumer acks (SQS visibility timeout, 30 s by default; RabbitMQ manual ack; Kafka offset commit after the work). A crash after the effect but before the ack, or a lost ack, makes the broker redeliver, so the effect runs again. Nothing is lost, duplicates are normal. This is the default of nearly every durable broker, and the producer has the same problem in miniature: a send whose ack is lost is retried and appends a second copy.

howItWorks.title: Why exactly-once delivery cannot exist
howItWorks.text: This is the Two Generals problem: the last message of any exchange can be lost, and the sender of that last message never learns whether it arrived. An ack cannot be acked forever, so at some point one side must decide to retry (risking a duplicate) or give up (risking a loss). What brokers sell as exactly-once is a different, achievable thing: effectively-once, meaning at-least-once delivery combined with processing whose repeat is harmless.

howItWorks.title: Make the effect safe to repeat: dedupe or transact
howItWorks.text: Idempotent consumer: every message carries a stable business id (payment id, not the offset), and the consumer inserts that id into a dedupe table with a unique constraint in the same database transaction as its result, so a redelivery hits the constraint and is skipped. Transactional consumer: write the result and the new offset in one transaction, so a crash leaves both or neither and the message is never redelivered. Kafka does the same inside the log: the idempotent producer (a producer id plus a per-partition sequence number the broker checks) removes producer retry duplicates, and transactions commit output records and consumed offsets atomically, with read_committed readers hiding aborted data.

howItWorks.title: Where the guarantee ends: external side effects
howItWorks.text: Kafka transactions, a database transaction or a dedupe table only cover state they own. An email, a card charge or a call to another service happens outside that transaction, so a crash between the call and the commit repeats it on retry. Such effects need their own idempotency key (Stripe-style Idempotency-Key = the payment id, remembered by the provider for about 24 hours), or an outbox so the effect is recorded in your transaction and sent by a relay that retries safely.

howItWorks.title: Choose by the cost of a lost versus a repeated message
howItWorks.text: Loss tolerable and rate high: at-most-once. Repeat harmless by nature (set status = shipped, upsert by key): plain at-least-once. Repeat harmful: at-least-once plus an idempotent consumer, sized so the dedupe memory outlives the longest possible redelivery delay. Pipeline that stays inside one transactional store such as Kafka to Kafka: use its transactions. Always measure the redelivery rate in production; the duplicate path that never runs in testing is the one that bites.

pros: At-least-once with idempotent processing gives the correct final state without a distributed transaction
At-most-once is the cheapest and fastest option and is honest about what it drops
Making the guarantee explicit lets each consumer pick the cost it can afford
A transactional offset or dedupe table makes crash recovery a non-event: restart and carry on
cons: Exactly-once is a property of a whole pipeline, not of the broker, and it breaks at the first external call
A dedupe store costs a write per message, storage, and an expiry policy
Transactions inside the log (Kafka) cost latency and throughput, and only protect Kafka-to-Kafka flows
Idempotent consumers must be designed in; retrofitting them onto a handler that sends emails is painful
whenToUse: At-least-once plus an idempotent consumer: money, inventory, orders, anything where a repeat or a loss is a real error
Transactional offset and result: stream processing whose output and state live in one store
At-most-once: telemetry, sampled metrics, heartbeats, cache invalidation hints where a newer message will fix it
whenNotToUse: Do not build dedupe machinery for operations that are naturally idempotent, such as set-status or upsert by key
Do not use at-most-once for anything a person would notice missing
Do not pay for broker transactions when the consumer only calls external services, since the transaction cannot cover them
Do not trust a marketing claim of exactly-once without asking what the boundary of the guarantee is
pitfalls: Deduplicating on the offset or message id instead of a business id: a producer retry creates a second message with a new offset and passes straight through
Writing the dedupe record in a separate transaction from the result, so a crash between the two either repeats the effect or loses it
A dedupe window shorter than the longest redelivery delay (a long visibility timeout, a consumer outage, a replay): the duplicate arrives after the id was forgotten
Committing the offset on a timer (auto-commit) rather than after the work, which silently turns at-least-once into at-most-once for the messages in flight
Treating an exactly-once checkbox on the broker as covering the email or the card charge the handler also performs
A poison message that always crashes the consumer under at-least-once is redelivered forever and blocks the partition, so it needs a retry limit and a dead-letter queue

roles.label: Producer
roles.description: Publishes payment events and retries when its send is not acknowledged.

roles.label: Broker
roles.description: Stores the log, tracks the committed offset and redelivers anything not acknowledged.

roles.label: Consumer
roles.description: Reads events, applies their effects and acknowledges, and can crash at any step.

roles.label: Ledger DB
roles.description: The consumer's own database: ledger rows, a dedupe table and optionally the offset, committed atomically.

roles.label: Card API
roles.description: An external service outside the transaction, which needs its own idempotency key.
